title: Optimising Surface Area and Volume — Year 9

header.title: Optimising Surface Area and Volume
header.subtitle: Same volume, less material: which shape wins?

meta.lesson-focus: Investigate optimisation problems — prisms with the same volume but different surface areas; can-cooler material minimisation; conjecture and test which shapes give the smallest surface area for a given volume; First Nations objects/technologies as SA-volume contexts.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: solve problems involving the volume and surface area of right prisms and cylinders using appropriate units
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Spatial relationships in 1, 2 and 3 dimensions can be quantified using appropriate units to solve problems in various contexts

html.section0_intro: Last lesson you found the volume and surface area of cylinders; before that, right prisms. Today you put both together. These three questions check the skills you need.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's measurement.

A cereal company needs a box that holds 1000 cm³. One designer suggests a long, flat box 20 cm × 5 cm × 10 cm. Another suggests a 10 cm cube.

Both hold exactly the same cereal. But the flat box needs 700 cm² of card and the cube only 600 cm². At $0.002 per cm², that is 20 cents saved per box, or $2000 on a run of 10 000 boxes.

Same volume, different surface area. Today you investigate which shapes hold a fixed volume using the least material, make a conjecture, and test it on boxes, cans and can-coolers.

html.worked_example:
Explore first. Every box below holds exactly 64 cm³ and has a square base. Drag the slider to change the base side x; the height changes so the volume stays 64 cm³. Watch the surface area.

Base: 2 × 2 cm
Height h = 64 ÷ x² = 16 cm
Volume = 64 cm³
SA = 2x² + 4xh = 136 cm²

🎯 Challenge

Set the slider to the base side that uses the least card, then press Check.

Now prove it. Compare two boxes that each hold 64 cm³: a 4 cm cube and a 8 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm box.

1
Check the volumes match
We can only compare fairly if both boxes hold the same amount.
Cube: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³
Box: 8 × 2 × 4 = 64 cm³
2
Find each surface area
Three pairs of faces: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh).
Cube: 6 × 16 = 96 cm²
Box: 2 × (16 + 32 + 8) = 112 cm²
3
Compare and conjecture
The cube needs 16 cm² less card. The slider showed the same thing: the lowest point on the graph is at x = 4, the cube.
Conjecture For a fixed volume, the box closest to a cube has the smallest surface area.

html.strategy_section:
★Hinge check🎯 Pick one

Before the exit ticket: one question, four answers. Each wrong answer points to a different mistake.

A 4 cm cube (surface area 96 cm²) and a 16 cm × 1 cm × 4 cm box both hold 64 cm³. What is the surface area of the 16 cm × 1 cm × 4 cm box?
That is the volume, not the surface area. 16 × 1 × 4 = 64 cm³ measures the space inside. Surface area adds up the areas of the six faces, in cm².
Same volume does not mean same surface area. That is the cube's surface area. Work it out for this box: 2 × (16 + 64 + 4).
You found only half the faces. 16 + 64 + 4 = 84 counts one face from each pair. A box has two of each, so double it.
Correct. 2 × (16×1 + 16×4 + 1×4) = 2 × 84 = 168 cm², far more than the cube's 96 cm² for the same 64 cm³. Long, thin boxes waste card.

Can-cooler fundraiser. A foam sleeve wraps a can of radius 3.5 cm and height 12 cm, open at both ends. Foam costs $0.01 per cm². Using π = 3.14, what does the foam for 40 sleeves cost, in dollars?
practice2.hint: One sleeve is the curved surface only: 2 × 3.14 × 3.5 × 12 = 263.76 cm². Then × 0.01 × 40.

practice3.q: A box has a base 2 cm by 8 cm and holds the same volume as a 4 cm cube (64 cm³). How many more cm² of card does it need than the cube?
practice3.hint: Height = 64 ÷ 16 = 4 cm. Then SA = 2 × (16 + 8 + 32); the cube is 96 cm².

An open-top box (no lid) has a square base and holds 32 cm³. Try base sides 2 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm (heights 8 cm, 2 cm and 0.5 cm). What is the least area of card needed, in cm²?
practice3.hint: No lid: card = base + four sides = x² + 4xh. Base 4: 16 + 4×4×2.

practice3.q: A gift shop folds 200 boxes that each hold 216 cm³. A 6 cm cube needs 216 cm² of card; a 12 cm × 3 cm × 6 cm box needs 252 cm². Card costs $0.005 per cm². How many dollars does choosing the cube save across all 200 boxes?
practice3.hint: Saving per box in cm², × 200 boxes, × $0.005.
